issues.subcategory: cue timing confounded with report timing
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly interprets the short-delay conditions as memory reports obtained 0.5–0.75 s after stimulus offset, but in the described procedures participants often made the actual response only after a later irrelevant display. Thus the manipulation is primarily the timing of a retro-cue/probe, not the time at which memory is reported. This undermines claims that high-confidence illusions occur at the stated early time points and that increases across conditions reflect transformation of a stored representation over that exact interval.
issues.quote: "In all conditions, after offset of the second letter display, the participant first indicated the identity of the letter at the cued location in the memory display."

issues.description: The short and long conditions differ in when the target location is cued. An early cue can allow selective attention, consolidation, verbal recoding, or protection of the target before later interference, whereas a late cue requires maintaining the whole display longer. Therefore differences between short and long conditions may reflect retro-cue benefits or failures of attentional selection rather than progressive conversion of a correctly encoded pseudo-letter into a real-letter memory.
issues.quote: "In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display."

issues.subcategory: increase over time does not rule out perceptual or encoding errors
issues.description: The authors infer that an increase in errors over delay rules out perceptual encoding accounts. This is too strong. Encoding noise, weak orientation encoding, categorical/verbal recoding, retrieval bias, retro-cue effects, and decision bias can all interact with delay. Without an immediate perceptual report condition while the display is visible or immediately after offset, the study cannot establish that the initial percept was correct and later transformed in STM.
issues.quote: "If the illusions are simply the result of misperceptions, their frequency of occurrence should remain the same over the time-course of STM – since in all cases initial perceptual inference has been completed."

issues.description: The discussion claims that correctly encoded percepts are converted into illusory memories. The design measures forced-choice reports after delays and cannot directly observe encoding accuracy or memory-trace transformation. The data are also compatible with decay of orientation information plus canonical-letter response bias, differential discriminability, or retrieval reconstruction.
issues.quote: "Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter."

issues.subcategory: high confidence treated as proof of false memory
issues.description: The operational definition of an illusory memory relies on high confidence. High confidence does not establish the presence of a false memory trace; it may reflect response bias, metacognitive miscalibration, familiarity of real letters, or overconfident guessing. The manuscript therefore overinterprets confidence ratings as evidence that guessing and response bias have been excluded.
issues.quote: "we exclude the possibility that the errors are a result of guessing in the absence of reliable memories / reliable perception by focusing on high confidence errors: errors where the participant explicitly indicates to know the answer, and has not just guessed."

issues.description: The analyses depend entirely on classifying trials as high confidence, yet the manuscript never explicitly states whether 'high confidence' means rating 4 only, ratings 3–4, or some other rule. This is essential for replication and for evaluating the large participant exclusions based on high-confidence trial counts.
issues.quote: "After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes (from 1-4, 1 = guess, 4 = certain)."

issues.subcategory: large exclusions based on outcome-related confidence
issues.description: A substantial fraction of participants were excluded because they had too few high-confidence trials. Confidence is part of the dependent process and likely varies with memory ability, condition difficulty, and response strategy. Excluding low-confidence participants can bias error-rate estimates and limits conclusions to a selected high-confidence subgroup. No sensitivity analyses including all participants are reported.
issues.quote: "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)"

issues.description: Experiment 2 excludes 92 of 290 participants, nearly one third of the sample, based on high-confidence trial availability. Because excluded participants had much lower confidence, the analyzed sample is not representative of the recruited sample. The manuscript does not report whether the core effects hold when lower-confidence participants are modeled rather than excluded.
issues.quote: "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)"

issues.description: Analyzing only high-confidence trials conditions on a post-response variable that is itself affected by target type, delay, accuracy, and bias. This can induce selection/collider bias and distort condition comparisons. A more appropriate analysis would jointly model accuracy/error type and confidence, or include all trials with confidence as an outcome or predictor.
issues.quote: "error rates on high confidence trials were analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), memory delay (long or short) and error type"

issues.subcategory: ANOVA on bounded proportions with unequal denominators
issues.description: The primary analyses use repeated-measures ANOVAs on aggregated percentages/proportions. These outcomes are bounded, often based on small and unequal cell counts after high-confidence filtering, and have binomial/multinomial sampling variance. The analyses do not weight by denominator or model trial-level uncertainty. A binomial or multinomial mixed-effects model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: "The relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), interval (short or long) and type of error"

issues.description: The manuscript does not clearly define the denominator for reported error rates: all trials, high-confidence trials, high-confidence critical trials, trials in which the target was present, or trials in which the counterpart was present. This is especially problematic in Experiment 1, where response displays sometimes did not contain the true target. Without raw counts and denominators per cell, the reported percentages cannot be independently evaluated.
issues.quote: "For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated."

issues.description: The main test of whether illusions occur compares choosing the mirrored counterpart with selecting unrelated distractors. These are not equivalent error categories: the mirrored counterpart shares identity/shape with the target, whereas unrelated distractors do not, and the number of available alternatives in each category differs. A higher counterpart-selection rate therefore does not by itself demonstrate an illusory memory rather than similarity-based confusion or categorical response bias.
issues.quote: "hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? – by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors (main effect of Error Type)."

issues.description: Experiment 1 appears to describe response displays containing either the target or its mirror-reversed counterpart, not both. Later the manuscript describes critical trials as if the target was combined with its mirrored counterpart. This affects interpretation because selecting the mirrored item when the true target is absent is different from choosing it over the actually presented target.
issues.quote: "The response display consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed)"

issues.description: The manuscript says critical trials were those in which a target was combined with its mirrored counterpart, but the preceding description indicates that the response option was either the target or the mirrored counterpart. This makes it unclear which trials entered the critical analyses and whether participants had the correct target available as a response option.
issues.quote: "trials where participants could exhibit memory illusion: trials in which a real- or pseudo-letter target was combined with its mirrored counterpart in the response screen"

issues.description: The text states that, for non-illusory errors, Memory Delay was the only relevant factor and had BFincl = 190. However Table 4 reports BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay and BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type. This is a direct contradiction and suggests either table mislabeling, incorrect extraction of Bayes factors, or erroneous interpretation of the analysis.
issues.quote: "For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42... Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)"

issues.description: The actual Table 4 entries indicate evidence against including Memory Delay and strong evidence for Target Type, opposite to the narrative. This undermines the reported follow-up interpretation for Experiment 2 and potentially the claim that non-illusory errors increased similarly over time.

The manuscript says the increase was smaller for mirrored targets but then gives 5% for mirrored targets and 4% for real-letter targets. This is internally inconsistent and raises concerns about proofreading and interpretation of the interaction pattern.
issues.quote: "There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference)."

issues.description: Experiment 4 results refer to Figure 5, but the Experiment 4 figure is captioned Figure 6. This is a minor reporting inconsistency but may confuse readers and indicates insufficient manuscript checking.
issues.quote: "Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials."

issues.description: The general discussion states that memory was probed at 500 ms in Experiments 1 and 2, but Experiment 1 describes a 0.75 s short delay. This matters because the authors use the exact timing to argue that illusions arise extremely rapidly.
issues.quote: "Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)"

issues.description: The abstract describes the critical time frame as 1 or 2 seconds, but the experiments use 0.5/0.75 s and 3 s cue delays, with actual responses often later. The abstract therefore does not accurately summarize the experimental timing.
issues.quote: "within this timeframe, participants go from reliably reporting what was there"

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used sequential Bayes-factor stopping, but the manuscript does not specify the prior used for the monitored t-test, whether the test was one- or two-sided, the minimum and maximum sample sizes, the number/timing of interim looks beyond 'every other day', or whether the rule was preregistered. Optional stopping with incomplete specification increases analytic flexibility and impairs interpretability.
issues.quote: "Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop."

issues.subcategory: sample-size stopping based on a different test than main analysis
issues.description: The stopping rule was based on a 'critical t-test' comparing the effect of Error Type for real and pseudo-letter targets, but the primary reported analyses are Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVAs and Experiment 4 also tests delay effects. Stopping on one effect can yield poorly calibrated evidence for other reported effects, especially the Memory Delay × Error Type hypothesis.
issues.quote: "Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test, namely the comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets."

issues.subcategory: underpowered and unstable Experiment 1 after exclusions
issues.description: Experiment 1 analyzes only 23 participants after excluding 17 from the main experiment, leaving small within-cell counts for a three-factor repeated-measures design. This makes Experiment 1's interaction estimates unstable, especially for high-confidence critical trials, and the manuscript does not report an a priori power or precision analysis.
issues.quote: "resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)"

issues.description: The large sample in Experiment 2 was determined by course enrollment rather than power, precision, or a stopping rule. While large N is not itself problematic, the manuscript provides no justification that the design had adequate trial counts per condition after high-confidence filtering, especially for the cue-color manipulation.
issues.quote: "The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course"

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 set size omitted from analysis
issues.description: Experiment 1 manipulated set size, but the reported analysis averages across set-size conditions and does not report whether set size affected accuracy, confidence, or illusions. Because memory load is central to STM decay and errors, omitting this factor creates an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom and may obscure important interactions.
issues.quote: "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions."

issues.description: Bayes factors are sensitive to prior choices and model specifications. The manuscript names JASP and describes BF interpretation thresholds but does not report the prior distributions, r-scale, model priors, or nuisance-prior settings used in the Bayesian ANOVAs and t-tests. This limits reproducibility and evaluation of the evidence.
issues.quote: "The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4"

issues.description: Experiment 1's key Memory Delay × Error Type evidence is BFincl = 4.21, which the authors treat as support for the time/decay hypothesis. This is only modest evidence and does not justify strong language that the experiment clearly demonstrates an increase of illusions with memory deterioration, especially given exclusions and aggregation.
issues.quote: "The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2"

issues.subcategory: collapsing cue-color analysis over memory delay
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the cue-color manipulation was tested only with target type and cue color, apparently omitting memory delay. If transient expectations influence memory specifically at longer delays, collapsing over delay could mask the theoretically relevant effect. The decision to collapse over cue type for all later analyses should have been justified with a full model including delay and interactions.
issues.quote: "analysing the illusory error rates (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter) and cue colour (red or blue, indicating low and high probability of a pseudoletter target) as factors."

issues.description: The red and blue fixation/cue colors differed substantially in luminance. Any effect or null effect of cue color could be confounded with visibility, salience, attention, or display calibration rather than expectation. This is especially relevant because color was used as the manipulation of transient expectation.
issues.quote: "blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2)."

issues.subcategory: no behavioral manipulation check for cue-probability learning
issues.description: The conclusion that transiently induced expectations failed to affect memory assumes participants learned and used the color-probability relationship. The only check was an open-ended post-experiment questionnaire, which assesses explicit awareness poorly and does not test implicit learning. Accuracy, response bias, or RT evidence by color over time would be needed.
issues.quote: "The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses."

issues.subcategory: unsupported inference from null cue-color effect
issues.description: The authors infer from a null cue-color effect that expectations may need substantial time to develop. Because the manipulation may not have been learned, was confounded with color/luminance, and may have been underpowered after high-confidence exclusions, this theoretical conclusion is not warranted.
issues.quote: "This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories."

issues.subcategory: verbal recoding and orientation-feature load confound
issues.description: Real letters can be encoded verbally by identity alone, whereas pseudo-letters require encoding identity plus mirror orientation. A pseudo-to-real response may arise when the orientation feature is forgotten but the verbal letter identity remains, not because world knowledge reshaped a visual STM trace. The experiments do not include articulatory suppression or other controls for verbal labeling.
issues.quote: "Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right). Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment"

issues.description: The key comparison between real and mirrored letters confounds prior knowledge with familiarity, nameability, perceptual discriminability, and memory strength. The observed asymmetry may reflect easier maintenance of canonical forms or poorer orientation binding for pseudo-letters rather than a top-down world-knowledge-driven illusion.
issues.quote: "All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet."

issues.subcategory: world-knowledge causal claim not experimentally isolated
issues.description: The authors claim that world knowledge drives the effects because pseudo-to-real errors exceed real-to-pseudo errors. However, world knowledge was not independently manipulated; target type also changes familiarity, verbal encodability, orientation complexity, and response bias. Thus the causal attribution to world knowledge is stronger than the design supports.
issues.quote: "The interaction between Target Type and Error Type (BFincl >1000) provides evidence for Hypothesis 3"

issues.subcategory: response-bias alternative not adequately ruled out
issues.description: The manuscript argues that response bias is unlikely because pseudo-to-real errors are more common at high than low confidence, but no formal signal-detection or multinomial model of response bias is reported. High-confidence response bias toward familiar real letters remains plausible, especially in forced-choice displays where real letters are more nameable and familiar.
issues.quote: "If the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias... should be present not only for the high-confidence responses; indeed, it should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses."

issues.subcategory: low-confidence response-bias analysis not fully reported
issues.description: The response-bias rebuttal relies on low-confidence error percentages, but this analysis is not described in the Methods, no statistical test is reported, and the denominators are unclear. It is therefore difficult to evaluate whether the low-confidence pattern meaningfully rules out bias.
issues.quote: "On high confidence trials pseudo-letter targets were more often confused for their real counterparts (36%) than on low confidence trials (22%). However, the reverse was observed when real letter targets were confused for their pseudo counterpart (high confidence: 11%, low confidence: 17%)."

issues.description: The manuscript does not sufficiently specify the exact letter set, font, letter size, case, anti-aliasing, display equipment, refresh rate, resolution, viewing distance, or calibration procedures for the main experiments. These details are crucial for 250 ms visual displays and mirror-letter discrimination and are necessary for replication.
issues.quote: "The memory and cue displays were set up in the same way as the displays in the training session, with 6 or 8 letters replacing the tilted bars."

issues.subcategory: online timing and viewing conditions uncontrolled
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online on participants' own laptops while connected via Zoom. The manuscript does not report controls for viewing distance, screen size, refresh rate, browser timing accuracy, dropped frames, or display scaling. Because the critical stimulus presentation is 250 ms and involves small visual differences, uncontrolled online timing and geometry threaten comparability with laboratory experiments.
issues.quote: "the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting . Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting... given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 4 timing underspecified after procedure change
issues.description: Experiment 4 says it is identical to Experiment 3 except for adding short and long cue intervals and moving online. Because Experiment 3 had only a 3 s cue interval inherited from Experiment 2, it is unclear exactly when the irrelevant second display occurred in the new short-interval trials and how long participants maintained the cued item before response.
issues.quote: "The procedure was identical to Experiment 3, with 2 exceptions. First, the interval between the memory display and the cue was either 500 ms (short interval) or 3000 ms (long interval)."

issues.description: Experiment 3 first excludes participants for too few high-confidence trials, then excludes another participant because of missing cells. This indicates that the exclusion procedure did not fully address sparse cells and that final analyzed N is ambiguous. Missing high-confidence cells are unlikely to be missing completely at random.
issues.quote: "Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA."

issues.description: The manuscript reports inclusion of 59 participants after exclusions but then says one more participant was excluded from the main ANOVA. The Results do not clearly state whether N = 59 or N = 58 for the reported Bayes factors.
issues.quote: "resulted in an inclusion of 59 participants (5 participants were excluded)... one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA."

issues.subcategory: feedback may alter expectations and strategies
issues.description: Participants received trial-by-trial or block feedback, which could change strategies, response biases, awareness of target probabilities, and treatment of pseudo-letters over time. The manuscript does not model learning or order effects, despite making claims about world knowledge versus experiment-long exposure.
issues.quote: "After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance. The main experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 20 trials. After each block the participant received feedback on her performance"

issues.description: The results are interpreted as support for predictive processing, but the design does not distinguish predictive-processing integration from signal-detection bias, categorical memory, verbal recoding, source-monitoring errors, or ordinary Bayesian decision at retrieval. The theoretical framing is plausible but overclaimed relative to the evidence.
issues.quote: "Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions"

issues.subcategory: overstated rejection of fuzzy trace theory
issues.description: The manuscript argues that fuzzy trace theory cannot account for the findings based on a broad claim about similarity inhibiting false memories. The experiments do not directly test FTT mechanisms, gist/verbatim representations, or semantic versus perceptual gist, so this theoretical dismissal is not warranted.
issues.quote: "Therefore, it seems that FTT cannot accurately account for the occurrence of this type of memory illusions in STM."

issues.subcategory: overclaim to all stages of STM
issues.description: The manuscript claims all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories, but the experiments do not directly isolate iconic memory, fragile memory, and working memory. The tasks use delayed cues, forced-choice reports, possible verbal recoding, and delays mainly around 0.5–3 s. Claims about all STM stages exceed the evidence.
issues.quote: "The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research"

issues.subcategory: overclaim to visual percepts in general
issues.description: The experiments use a narrow stimulus class: familiar alphabetic symbols and their mirror reversals. The manuscript extrapolates to visual percepts in general, but the effect may depend on literacy, canonical letter orientation, verbal labeling, and symbol familiarity.
issues.quote: "it would suggest that memory biases are not limited to letters, but instead apply to (visual) percepts in general."

issues.description: Participants are mostly young University of Amsterdam psychology students, often predominantly female, and presumably highly familiar with the Latin alphabet. The manuscript makes broad claims about STM and memory generally without adequately limiting conclusions to similar literate young-adult samples.
issues.quote: "The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum."

issues.description: Because the theoretical manipulation depends on lifelong experience with the alphabet, the manuscript should report participants' native language, alphabet familiarity, reading direction, dyslexia/reading impairments, and exclusion criteria related to literacy. These are not described, limiting interpretation of the 'world knowledge' account.
issues.quote: "Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form."

issues.subcategory: main-effect test insufficient for occurrence claim
issues.description: The manuscript treats a main effect of Error Type as evidence that illusions occur in STM. But occurrence should be assessed against a defined chance or baseline model that accounts for response-option structure, not merely against unrelated errors. This conflates presence of errors with relative prevalence over a non-equivalent error category.
issues.quote: "Hypothesis 1 would be supported if expectation-induced errors are more prevalent than other errors, resulting in a main effect of Error Type."

issues.description: Several results report follow-up Bayes-factor t-tests, but the manuscript does not specify whether tests were paired, one- or two-sided, what priors were used, or how multiple follow-ups were planned. This limits reproducibility and interpretation of reported BFs.
issues.quote: "BF>1000 in a follow-up t-test"

issues.subcategory: interference condition confounds memory decay with cue/perceptual interference
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the Short-with-interference condition presents the cue together with the irrelevant second display. This may impair cue processing, spatial attention, or perceptual selection rather than specifically increasing memory decay. Therefore interpreting this condition as memory deterioration through interference is ambiguous.
issues.quote: "If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition)."

issues.subcategory: confidence rating after forced-choice response may reflect decision certainty
issues.description: Confidence was collected after participants selected among response options. Such ratings may index confidence in the forced-choice decision or familiarity of the selected option, not necessarily subjective recollection of the original display. This weakens the interpretation of high-confidence errors as 'the illusory experience of a reliable and reportable memory.'
issues.quote: "After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes"

issues.subcategory: balanced stimulus set does not eliminate response bias
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 balance the frequency of real and pseudo-letters within the experiment, but this does not eliminate differential familiarity, verbal labeling, or response preference for canonical letters. Thus the continued pseudo-to-real asymmetry cannot be uniquely attributed to lifelong world knowledge.
issues.quote: "when letters and pseudo-letters are just as prevalent, participants still show the same pattern of results"
